entities.name: Diego Lopez de Pacheco, 2nd Duke of Escalona
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Diego López de Pacheco, 2nd Duke of Escalona and 2nd Marquis of Villena, was a formidable Castilian grandee whose life, from his birth in an unknown year to his death on November 26, 1529, spanned the tumultuous transition from the late medieval period to the consolidation of the early modern Spanish monarchy. As one of the most powerful nobles in Castile, holding vast estates centered in the region of Cuenca and Toledo, his actions directly impacted the political stability of the kingdom during the regency of Ferdinand II of Aragon and the early reign of Emperor Charles V. His defiance of royal authority, particularly during periods of succession crisis, positioned him as a central figure in the ongoing struggle between the crown and the entrenched Castilian aristocracy.

Pacheco inherited his immense titles and patrimony from his father, Juan Pacheco, 1st Duke of Escalona, a key figure under Henry IV. Diego himself became a prominent, often recalcitrant, magnate, asserting his feudal rights against the centralizing efforts of the Catholic Monarchs. Following the death of Isabella I in 1504, he initially sided with Philip I, then later opposed Ferdinand II's regency, leveraging his extensive network of vassals and fortified strongholds. His most significant involvement came during the War of the Comuneros (1520-1522), where he initially displayed ambiguous loyalty but eventually aligned with the rebel Comuneros, providing military support and strategic counsel, particularly around Toledo. Despite his initial resistance, he was eventually pardoned by Charles V after the royalist victory at Villalar.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Diego López de Pacheco was a pivotal figure in the early 16th-century struggle between the Castilian crown and its most powerful nobility, influencing the outcome of the Comuneros Revolt and shaping the relationship between the monarchy and grandees for centuries. His career exemplifies the definitive shift in power towards a centralized state in Spain.
